entries.ea36a1712d6e66d49d3863f647ca347c90869b2e: <div sID="gen13075" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="134" osisID="Ps.134" sID="Ps.134"/> <div eID="gen13075" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13076" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen13077" type="x-p"/> This is the last of the fifteen songs of degrees; and, if they were at any time sung all together in the temple-service, it is fitly made the conclusion of them, for the design of it is to stir up the ministers to go on with their work in the night, when the solemnities of the day were over. Some make this psalm to be a dialogue. I. In the <reference osisRef="Ps.134.1-Ps.134.2">first two verses</reference>, the priests or Levites who sat up all night to keep the watch of the house of the Lord are called upon to spend their time while they were upon the guard, not in idle talk, but in the acts of devotion. II. In the <reference osisRef="Ps.134.3">last verse</reference> those who were thus called upon to praise God pray for him that gave them the exhortation, either the high priest or the captain of the guard. Or thus: those who did that service did mutually exhort one another and pray for one another. In singing this psalm we must both stir up ourselves to give glory to God and encourage ourselves to hope for mercy and grace from him.
entries.d5b4f17ff76a0200b7ae80c1a260dca11bab7956: <div eID="gen13077" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen13076" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">A Call to Bless God.</title> <div sID="gen13078" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Behold, bless ye the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , all <hi type="italic">ye</hi> servants of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , which by night stand in the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">2</hi> Lift up your hands <hi type="italic">in</hi> the sanctuary, and bless the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">3</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> that made heaven and earth bless thee out of Zion. <div eID="gen13078" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13079" type="x-p"/> This psalm instructs us concerning a two-fold blessing:— <div eID="gen13079" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13080" type="x-p"/> I. Our blessing God, that is, speaking well of him, which here we are taught to do, <reference osisRef="Ps.134.1-Ps.134.2">v. 1, 2</reference>. 1. It is a call to the <hi type="italic">Levites</hi> to do it. They were <hi type="italic">the servants of the Lord</hi> by office, appointed to minister in holy things; they attended the sanctuary, and kept the charge of the house of the Lord, <reference osisRef="Num.3.6-Num.3.10">Num. iii. 6</reference>, &c. Some of them did <hi type="italic">by night stand in the house of the Lord,</hi> to guard the holy things of the temple, that they might not be profaned, and the rich things of the temple, that they might not be plundered. While the ark was in curtains there was the more need of guards upon it. They attended likewise to see that neither the fire on the altar nor the lamps in the candlestick went out. Probably it was usual for some devout and pious Israelites to sit up with them; we read of one that <hi type="italic">departed not from the temple night or day,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.2.37">Luke ii. 37</reference>. Now these are here called upon to <hi type="italic">bless the Lord.</hi> Thus they must keep themselves awake by keeping themselves employed. Thus they must redeem time for holy exercises; and how can we spend our time better than in praising God? It would be an excellent piece of husbandry to fill up the vacancies of time with pious meditations and ejaculations; and surely it is a very modest and reasonable to converse with God when we have nothing else to do. Those who stood <hi type="italic">in the house of the Lord</hi> must remember where they were, and that holiness and holy work became that house. Let them therefore <hi type="italic">bless the Lord;</hi> let them all do it in concert, or each by himself; let them <hi type="italic">lift up</hi> their <hi type="italic">hands</hi> in the doing of it, in token of the lifting up of their hearts. <hi type="italic">Let them lift up their hands in holiness</hi> (so Dr. Hammond reads it) or in sanctification, as it is fit when they lift them up <hi type="italic">in the sanctuary;</hi> and let them remember that when they were appointed to wash before they went in to minister they were thereby taught to <hi type="italic">lift up holy hands</hi> in prayer and praise. 2. It is a call to us to do it, who, as Christians, are made priests to our God, and Levites, <reference osisRef="Isa.66.21">Isa. lxvi. 21</reference>. We are the <hi type="italic">servants of the Lord;</hi> we have a place and a name in his house, in his sanctuary; we stand before him to minister to him. Even by night we are under his eye and have access to him. Let us therefore <hi type="italic">bless the Lord,</hi> and again bless him; think and speak of his glory and goodness. Let us <hi type="italic">lift up</hi> our <hi type="italic">hands</hi> in prayer, in praise, in vows; let us do our work with diligence and cheerfulness, and an elevation of mind. This exhortation is ushered in with <hi type="italic">Behold!</hi> a note commanding attention. Look about you, Sirs, when you are in God's presence, and conduct yourselves accordingly. <div eID="gen13080" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13081" type="x-p"/> II. God's blessing us, and that is doing well for us, which we are here taught to desire, <reference osisRef="Ps.134.3">v. 3</reference>. Whether it is the watchmen's blessing their captain, or the Levites' blessing the high priest, or whoever was their chief (as many take it, because it is in the singular number, <hi type="italic">The Lord bless thee</hi>), or whether the blessing is pronounced by one upon many ("<hi type="italic">The Lord bless thee,</hi> each of you in particular, thee and thee; you that are blessing God, the Lord bless you"), is not material. We may learn, 1. That we need desire no more to make us happy than to be blessed of the Lord, for those whom he blesses are blessed indeed. 2. That blessings out of Zion, spiritual blessings, the blessings of the covenant, and of communion with God, are the best blessings, which we should be most earnest for. 3. It is a great encouragement to us, when we come to God for a blessing, that it is he who <hi type="italic">made heaven and earth,</hi> and therefore has all the blessings of both at his disposal, the upper and nether springs. 4. We ought to beg these blessings, not only for ourselves, but for others also; not only, The Lord bless <hi type="italic">me,</hi> but, The Lord bless <hi type="italic">thee,</hi> thus testifying our belief of the fulness of divine blessings, that there is enough for others as well as for us, and our good-will also to others. We must pray for those that exhort us. Though <hi type="italic">the less is blessed of the greater</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.7.7">Heb. vii. 7</reference>), yet the greater must be prayed for by the less.  <chapter eID="Ps.134"/> <div eID="gen13081" type="x-p"/>

entries.beea503974e76c0e404bbd8ea2b06f79e1fbbb20: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7050"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 134</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.134.1-Ps.3.1">Psa 134:1-3. 1</reference>, 2. The pilgrim bands arriving at the sanctuary call on the priests, who</title> <div sID="gen10816" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stand in the house of the Lord--</hi>at the time of the evening sacrifice, to unite in praising God in their name and that of the people, using appropriate gestures, to which the priests reply, pronouncing the Mosaic blessing which they alone could pronounce. A fit epilogue to the whole pilgrim-book, Psalms 120-134.<div eID="gen10816" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10817" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by night--</hi>the evening service (<reference osisRef="Ps.141.2">Psa 141:2</reference>), as opposed to morning (<reference osisRef="Ps.92.2">Psa 92:2</reference>).<div eID="gen10817" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10818" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7050"/><hi type="bold">2. Lift up your hands--</hi>(Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.28.2">Psa 28:2</reference>). <div eID="gen10818" type="x-p"/>
entries.5d50045303f133aa59ca86207db14d2e894ad491: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7051"/><div sID="gen10819" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7051"/>3. After the manner directed (<reference osisRef="Num.6.23">Nu 6:23</reference>).<div eID="gen10819" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10820" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">out of Zion--</hi>the Church, as His residence, and thus seat of blessings. Thus close the songs of degrees. <chapter eID="Ps.134"/>

entries.30160745ece5d1a62e1de2c5544bddf114e8e395: <div eID="gen23213" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen23214" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen23215" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen23215" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen23214" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen23216" type="x-p"/> An exhortation to praise God in his sanctuary, <reference osisRef="Psa.134.1-Psa.134.3">Psa 134:1-3</reference>. <div eID="gen23216" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23217" type="x-p"/> This is the last of the fifteen Psalms called Psalms of degrees. Who was the author is uncertain; it is attributed to David only by the Syriac; it is intimately connected with the two preceding Psalms, and is an exhortation to the priests and Levites who kept nightly watch in the temple, to the assiduous in praising the Lord. It seems to consist of two parts: 1. An exhortation, probably from the high priest, to those priests and Levites who kept watch in the temple by night, to spend their time profitably, and duly celebrate the praises of God, <reference osisRef="Psa.134.1">Psa 134:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.134.2">Psa 134:2</reference>. The second part, which is contained in the <reference osisRef="Psa.134.3">Psa 134:3</reference>, is the prayer of the priests and Levites for the high priest, who seems now to be going to his rest. <div eID="gen23217" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23218" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen23218" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23219" type="x-p"/> Behold, bless ye the Lord - I believe הנה hinneh should be taken here in the sense of take heed! Be upon your guard; you serve a jealous God; provoke him not. <div eID="gen23219" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23220" type="x-p"/> Which by night stand - Who minister during the night.
entries.472122d0923cdbb8a52f3216f565095247436f39: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen23220" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23221" type="x-p"/> Lift up your hands in the sanctuary - קדש kodesh, "in holiness:" or, as the Syriac, lekoudishe, "to holiness;" in sancta, Vulgate; and εις τα ἁγια, Septuagint; "in holy things; or, as the Aethiopic, in the house of the sanctuary." The expression seems very similar to that of St. Paul, <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.8">1Tim 2:8</reference> : "Lifting up holy hands, without wrath and doubting." <div eID="gen23221" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23222" type="x-p"/> Bless the Lord - That is, speak good of his name: tell the wonders he has wrought, and show that his name is exalted.
entries.250ee3d3cfb76378de8e8b4f33860152a5685c9d: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen23222" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23223" type="x-p"/> The Lord that made heaven and earth - Who governs and possesses all things; and who can give you every spiritual and earthly blessing. <div eID="gen23223" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23224" type="x-p"/> Bless thee out of Zion - As if they had said, "We will attend to your orders; go in peace, and may God shower down his blessings upon you!" The blessing pronounced by the priests was the following: "The Lord bless thee and keep thee! The Lord make his face shine upon thee, and he gracious unto thee! The Lord lift up his countenance upon thee, and give thee peace!" <reference osisRef="Num.6.24-Num.6.26">Num 6:24-26</reference>.  <chapter eID="Ps.134"/> <div eID="gen23224" type="x-p"/>

entries.9e119913304b1fee7c6a44932622a781be10d5bc: <div eID="gen10239" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Night-Watch Greeting and Counter-Greeting</title> <div sID="gen10240" type="x-p"/> This Psalm consists of a greeting, <reference osisRef="Ps.134.1-Ps.134.2">Psa 134:1-2</reference>, and the reply thereto. The greeting is addressed to those priests and Levites who have the night-watch in the Temple; and this antiphon is purposely placed at the end of the collection of Songs of degrees in order to take the place of a final beracha. In this sense Luther styles this Psalm <hi type="italic">epiphonema superiorum</hi>. It is also in other respects (vid., <hi type="italic">Symbolae</hi>, p. 66) an appropriate finale.
entries.efbe09c10f4d4c8e56740eec7c9b71f8f234da50: <reference osisRef="Ps.134.1-Ps.134.2">Psa 134:1-2</reference> <div eID="gen10240" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10241" type="x-p"/> The Psalm begins, like its predecessor, with הנּה; there is directs attention to an attractive phenomenon, here to a duty which springs from the office. For that it is not the persons frequenting the Temple who are addressed is at once clear from the fact that the tarrying of these in the Temple through the night, when such a thing did actually occur (<reference osisRef="Luke.2.37">Luk 2:37</reference>), was only an exception. And then, however, from the fact that עמד is the customary word for the service of the priests and Levites, <reference osisRef="Deut.10.8">Deu 10:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.18.7">Deu 18:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.23.30">1Ch 23:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.29.11">2Ch 29:11</reference> (cf. on <reference osisRef="Isa.61.10">Isa 61:10</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Ps.110.4">Psa 110:4</reference>), which is also continued in the night, 1Ch 9:33. Even the Targum refers <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.134.1">Psa 134:1</reference></hi> to the Temple-watch. In the second Temple the matter was arranged thus. After midnight the chief over the gate-keepers took the keys of the inner Temple and went with some of the priests through the little wicket of the Fire Gate (שׁער בית המוקד). In the inner court this patrol divided into two companies, each with a burning torch; one company turned west, the other east, and so they compassed the court to see whether everything was in readiness for the service of the dawning day. At the bakers’ chamber, in which the <hi type="italic">Mincha</hi> of the high priest was baked (לשׁכת עשׂי הביתין), they met with the cry: All is well. In the meanwhile the rest of the priests also arose, bathed, and put on their garments. Then they went into the stone chamber (one half of which was the place of session of the Sanhedrim), where, under the superintendence of the chief over the drawing of the lots and of a judge, around whom stood all the priests in their robes of office, the functions of the priests in the service of the coming day were assigned to them by lot (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.9">Luk 1:9</reference>). Accordingly Tholuck, with Köster, regards Psa 134:1. and <reference osisRef="Ps.134.3">Psa 134:3</reference> as the antiphon of the Temple-watch going off duty and those coming on. It might also be the call and counter-call with which the watchmen greeted one another when they met. But according to the general keeping of the Psalm, Psa 134:1. have rather to be regarded as a call to devotion and intercession, which the congregation addresses to the priests and Levites entrusted with the night-service in the Temple. It is an error to suppose that “in the nights” can be equivalent to “early and late.” If the Psalter contains Morning Psalms (<reference osisRef="Ps.3.1-Ps.3.8">Psa 3:1-8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.63.1-Ps.63.11">Psa 63:1-11</reference>) and Evening Psalms (<reference osisRef="Ps.4.1-Ps.4.8">Psa 4:1-8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.141.1-Ps.141.10">Psa 141:1-10</reference>), why should it then not contain a vigil Psalm? On this very ground Venema’s idea too, that בּלּילות is syncopated from בּהלּילות, “with <hi type="italic">Hallels</hi>, i.e., praises,” is useless. Nor is there any reason for drawing ἐν ταῖς νυξίν, as the lxx does, to <reference osisRef="Ps.134.2">Psa 134:2</reference>,<note placement="foot">The lxx adjusts the shortening of <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.134.1">Psa 134:1</reference></hi> arising from this, by reading בחצרות בית אלהינו העמדים בבית ה after Psa 135:2.</note> or, what would be more natural, to the בּרכוּ that opens the Psalm, since it is surely not strange that, so long as the sanctuary was standing, a portion of the servants of God who ministered in it had to remain up at night to guard it, and to see to it that nothing was wanting in the preparations for the early service. That this ministering watching should be combined with devotional praying is the purport of the admonition in Psa 134:2. Raising suppliant hands (ידכם, negligently written for ידיכם) towards the Most Holy Place (τὰ ἅγια), they are to bless Jahve. קדשׁ (according to <hi type="italic">B. Sota 39a</hi>, the accusative of definition: in holiness, i.e., after washing of hands), in view of <reference osisRef="Ps.28.2">Psa 28:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.5.8">Psa 5:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.138.2">Psa 138:2</reference> (cf. רום in <reference osisRef="Hab.3.10">Hab 3:10</reference>), has to be regarded as the accusative of the direction.
entries.de5d39da72cb3230d8a9bfbad3e2ab1298c9f9fe: <reference osisRef="Ps.134.3">Psa 134:3</reference> <div eID="gen10241" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10242" type="x-p"/> Calling thus up to the Temple-hill, the church receives from above the benedictory counter-greeting: Jahve bless thee out of Zion (as in <reference osisRef="Ps.128.5">Psa 128:5</reference>), the Creator of heaven and earth (as in <reference osisRef="Ps.115.15">Psa 115:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.121.2">Psa 121:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.124.8">Psa 124:8</reference>). From the time of Num 6:24 <hi type="italic">jebaréchja</hi> is the ground-form of the priestly benediction. It is addressed to the church as one person, and to each individual in this united, unit-like church.  <chapter eID="Ps.134"/> <div eID="gen10242" type="x-p"/>

entries.7b85ce11e74f782949f9d2e9cbe6b64c20478304:
PSALM 134
An exhortation to praise God, addressed to the people of God generally, but more particularly to the Priests and Levites.
A Song of Degrees.
Psalm 134:1-3
1. Behold! bless ye Jehovah, all ye servants of Jehovah, who stand nightly in the house of Jehovah. 2. Lift up your hands towards the sanctuary,
“קדש. Some persons render this word as if it were an adverb. So Tilingins has ‘Attollite manus vestras sanete.’ There is no doubt, that lifting up the hands reverently, is the ordinary and proper posture of suppliants at the throne of grace. Farther, St. Paul, in 1 Timothy 2:8, apparently with reference to this passage, speaks of lifting up holy hands. The Septuagint and Syriac, however, have taken the word as a noun, signifying the sanctuary; the former have ἅγια.” ­ Phillips. Warner and Cress, well with Calvin would read “towards the sanctuary;” i.e., towards the holy of holies, where the ark, the symbol of the Divine presence, was fixed.
and bless Jehovah. 3. Jehovah bless thee out of Zion, who made heaven and earth!
 
1. Behold! bless ye Jehovah. Some interpreters think, that others besides the Levites are here intended, and it must be granted, at least, that some of the more zealous of the people remained over night in the Temple, as we read (Luke 2:37) of Anna, a widow, “who served God constantly with prayers night and day.”
“We know generally,” says Fry, “that there was a nightly service in the Temple, (2 Chronicles 21:) and Kimchi, a Jewish writer, represents those who by night stand in the house of the Lord, as holy men who rose from their beds in the night and went to pray in the Temple.” After referring to the case of “Anna, a Prophetess,” he adds, “And St. Paul, before Agrippa, speaking ‘of the hope of the promise made unto the fathers,’ gives us this remarkable description: ‘unto which our’ twelve tribes, instantly serving God day and night, hope to come. There was public service in the Temple at Jerusalem not only by day but by night; which latter service many of the Jews, for whose special use this and the next Psalm seem to have been composed, were in the habit of attending.” ­ Cresswell.
But it is evident, from the close of the Psalm, that the inspired penman addresses priests only, since he prescribes the form of benediction which they were to offer up for the people, and this was a duty belonging exclusively to the Priests. It would appear then, that the Levites are here called servants of God, from the functions they discharged, being specially appointed, and that by turns, to watch by night in the Temple, as we read in the inspired history.
Ye servants off the Lord, etc., i.e., ye Levites, whose duty it was, according to the Talmudists, to keep watch by night, standing in the Temple: the High Priest was the only one who sat in the Temple. Compare Leviticus 8:35; 1 Chronicles 9:33 Psalm 92:2; Psalm 119:147; Luke 2:37.” ­ Cresswell.
(Leviticus 8:35.) The Psalm begins with the demonstrative adverb Behold! setting the matter of their duty before their eyes, for they were to be stimulated to devotion by looking constantly to the Temple. We are to notice the Psalmist’s design in urging the duty of praise so earnestly upon them. Many of the Levites, through the tendency which there is in all men to abuse ceremonies, considered that nothing more was necessary than standing idly in the Temple, and thus overlooked the principal part of their duty. The Psalmist would show that merely to keep nightly watch over the Temple, kindle the lamps, and superintend the sacrifices, was of no importance, unless they served God spiritually, and referred all outward ceremonies to that which must be considered the main sacrifice ­ the celebration of God’s praises. You may think it a very laborious service, as if he had said, to stand at watch in the Temple, while others sleep in their own houses; but the worship which God requires is something more excellent than this, and demands of you to sing his praises before all the people. In the second verse he reminds them in addition, of the form observed in calling upon the name of the Lord. For why do men lift their hands when they pray? Is it not that their hearts may be raised at the same time to God?
“Car a quel propos les hommes eslevent ils les mains en priant, sinon afin qu’ils eslevent aussi leurs esprits a Dieu?” ­ Ft.
It is thus that the Psalmist takes occasion to reprehend their carelessness in either standing idle in the Temple, or trifling and indulging in vain conversation, and thus failing to worship God in a proper manner.

entries.3a3fcf9ec4e575d4fa635dc80054bf0b61be53a0:

                  <ns0:head>PSAL. CXXXIV.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:head>A song of degrees.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:argument>
                     <ns0:p>The form of this Psalm seems to be dramatical. In the two first verses the Psalmist speaks in the name of some eminent person, either the King or Chief Priest, exhorting and requiring all the Priests and Levites to perform the duties of their place and calling; and in the last verse in the name of the Priests and Levites returning him thanks for his good advice.</ns0:p>
                  </ns0:argument>
                  <ns0:p n="1">1 BEhold, bless ye the LORD <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Do not stand there like statues, dumb and idle, but employ your hearts and tongues in singing forth the praises of the Lord.</ns0:note> all <ns0:hi>ye</ns0:hi> ser<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vants of the LORD <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Peculiarly so called, Priests and Levites, who are set apart to the service of God and of the Sanctuary, as the next clause restrains this general expression.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> Chr. 9. 33.</ns0:note> which by night <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Not onely by day, but also and especially by night, when their watch was more necessary. See <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 27. 21. <ns0:hi>Levit.</ns0:hi> 8. 35. 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 3. 3. As you watch by night when others sleep, so do you utter the praises of God when others are silent.</ns0:note> stand <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Serve or minister, as this word is used <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 10. 8. & 18. 7. and oft elsewhere.</ns0:note> in the house <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Which word includes both the Temple and Courts belonging to it, as hath been noted before.</ns0:note> of the LORD.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 Lift up your hands <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Unto God in prayer and praises, thus expressing and exciting your inward devotion.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>, in <ns0:hi>holiness.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>in</ns0:hi> the sanctuary <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">In that holy house of God where you stand, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 1. Or, in or with <ns0:hi>holiness: Lift up your hands,</ns0:hi> as it is prescribed, 1 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 2. 8. Do not con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tent your selves with lifting up your hands, but see that this be done with pure and holy hearts.</ns0:note>: and bless the LORD.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 The LORD that made heaven and earth, bless thee <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Either, 1. thee whosoever thou ar<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">

                        </ns0:gap> who dost faithfully perform the duty here commanded.
